articles.title: Dark Horse: Dino levanta sigilo de investigação que cita Mário Frias, aponta indícios de irregularidades e menciona possível elo com PCC | G1
articles.standfirst: Dino vê indícios de conexão entre os inquéritos, cita a hipótese de uma organização criminosa voltada ao desvio de recursos públicos e menciona investigação sobre possíveis vínculos com o PCC. Na quinta-feira, Mário Frias classificou a operação da PF como uma 'cortina de fumaça'.
articles.summary: Dino vê indícios de conexão entre os inquéritos, cita a hipótese de uma organização criminosa voltada ao desvio de recursos públicos e menciona investigação sobre possíveis vínculos com o PCC. Na quinta-feira, Mário Frias classificou a operação da PF como uma 'cortina de fumaça'.
articles.body:
O ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Flávio Dino, levantou neste domingo (13) o sigilo de documentos enviados pela Justiça de São Paulo e unificou sob sua relatoria investigações que apuram um suposto esquema de desvio de recursos públicos envolvendo emendas parlamentares federais, contratos ligados à Prefeitura de São Paulo e pessoas vinculadas ao deputado federal Mário Frias (PL-SP).

Na última quinta-feira (10), Mario Frias classificou como “cortina de fumaça” a operação da PF que realizou buscas em sua residência. Em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais, o parlamentar negou irregularidades, afirmou que vai colaborar com as investigações e entregar todos os documentos necessários e disse acreditar no arquivamento do caso. Foi a primeira manifestação de Frias sobre a operação.

Na decisão divulgada neste domingo, Dino afirma haver indícios de conexão entre os inquéritos e menciona a hipótese investigativa de uma organização criminosa voltada à captação, circulação e ocultação de recursos públicos. O ministro também registra uma linha de investigação que apura possíveis vínculos do grupo investigado com a facção PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital).

Segundo o despacho, a Complexsys Soluções Integradas Ltda., empresa de tecnologia contratada pelo Instituto Conhecer Brasil (ICB), entidade presidida pela empresária Karina Ferreira da Gama e beneficiária de recursos oriundos de emendas parlamentares, recebeu transferências do deputado federal Mário Frias (PL-SP), que, segundo a Polícia Federal, teria papel central na suposta engrenagem investigada, e também repassou recursos de volta ao próprio instituto.

De acordo com o documento, a empresa ainda transferiu valores para a Academia Nacional de Cultura (ANC), organização sem fins lucrativos também presidida por Karina Gama. Para a Polícia Federal, a circulação de recursos entre Frias, a Complexsys, o ICB e a ANC sugere a existência de um "circuito financeiro fechado", compatível com a atuação coordenada de um mesmo núcleo.

"Essa circulação de recursos entre o parlamentar, a entidade executora, a empresa contratada e outra organização beneficiária não se compatibiliza com relações negociais independentes e economicamente justificadas. Ao contrário, evidencia um circuito financeiro fechado, característico de estruturas destinadas à circulação, fragmentação e reintrodução de valores entre integrantes de um mesmo núcleo de atuação", diz a representação da Polícia Federal citada no despacho.

Segundo a Polícia Federal, outro conjunto de evidências aponta para uma possível "confusão patrimonial" entre o Instituto Conhecer Brasil (ICB), empresas contratadas pela entidade e pessoas ligadas ao grupo investigado.

De acordo com a representação reproduzida no despacho de Flávio Dino, os investigadores identificaram vínculos societários cruzados, proximidade entre sócios e administradores, empresas com faturamento declarado incompatível com os valores movimentados e sucessivas devoluções de recursos sem justificativa econômica aparente. Para a PF, esses elementos indicam a possível atuação coordenada de pessoas físicas e jurídicas formalmente distintas.

"Tais circunstâncias afastam a hipótese de relações comerciais ordinárias e indicam, em tese, a utilização de pessoas jurídicas como instrumentos de circulação patrimonial e ocultação de valores. Em vez de agentes econômicos independentes contratando entre si em condições de mercado, o que se observa é a atuação coordenada de entes formalmente distintos, mas materialmente integrados por interesses comuns e por um fluxo financeiro sem justificativa negocial consistente", diz a representação da PF.

A Polícia Federal também aponta movimentações financeiras envolvendo o deputado federal Mário Frias e a empresa Go Up Entertainment, ligada à empresária Karina Ferreira da Gama. Segundo os investigadores, o parlamentar transferiu valores à empresa em montante que seria incompatível com sua renda declarada e com os créditos identificados nas contas bancárias analisadas.

Na avaliação da PF, essa circunstância afasta a hipótese de que Frias tenha atuado apenas como autor de emendas parlamentares posteriormente desviadas por terceiros. A representação reproduzida no despacho sustenta que as movimentações financeiras identificadas colocam o deputado como possível participante ativo da engrenagem financeira sob investigação.

Segundo os investigadores, Frias também mantinha relações patrimoniais com pessoas e empresas que integram o mesmo núcleo já identificado em outras frentes da apuração. Para a PF, esse conjunto de elementos reforça a hipótese de atuação articulada entre os investigados, embora os fatos ainda estejam sob investigação.

De acordo com o documento, essas informações levaram os investigadores à conclusão de que não há dois esquemas distintos, um relacionado ao desvio de recursos públicos no âmbito das emendas parlamentares e outro referente às movimentações financeiras de pessoas físicas e jurídicas vinculadas ao núcleo investigado, esteadas, na maior parte, em valores repassados ao ICB em decorrência do contrato firmado com a Prefeitura de São Paulo, objeto da investigação no âmbito da polícia judiciária estadual.

"Em verdade, há fortes indícios de uma única organização criminosa, estruturada para captar, disseminar e ocultar recursos provenientes de verbas públicas, na qual o Deputado Federal Mário Frias figura como agente central", afirma a representação da Polícia Federal reproduzida no despacho de Flávio Dino.

Ao analisar o material remetido pela Justiça de São Paulo, o ministro Flávio Dino avaliou que a investigação reforça a hipótese de existência de um esquema de destinação e desvio de recursos públicos envolvendo emendas parlamentares federais e contratos da Prefeitura de São Paulo.

No despacho, o ministro registra ainda que os autos mencionam uma linha de investigação segundo a qual a suposta organização criminosa teria possíveis vínculos com a facção PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital). Segundo Dino, trata-se de uma linha investigativa mencionada nos autos.

"Com efeito, no curso da investigação se fortalece a hipótese de imbricação indissociável em um sofisticado esquema de destinação e desvio de recursos públicos, com destaque para emendas parlamentares federais e para a prefeitura de São Paulo. Essa organização alcançaria, inclusive, vínculos com a facção PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), consoante linha investigativa mencionada nos autos", acrescentou o ministro, no despacho.

articles.title: Alleged trespasser stopped outside Kamala Harris’ Malibu home
articles.summary: An alleged trespasser was stopped by police on former Vice President Kamala Harris’ property in Malibu, California, Friday, officials said.
articles.body: An alleged trespasser was stopped by police on former Vice President Kamala Harris’ property in Malibu, California, Friday, officials said. The individual entered the property, where Harris and her husband, Doug Emhoff, live Friday night, but was stopped by security personnel before they reached the house itself, Eduardo Negrón, a spokesperson for Harris, said Saturday. “Vice President Harris and Second Gentleman Emhoff were not present. They are grateful to the security and law enforcement personnel who responded swiftly,” Negrón added. The Malibu Lost Hills Sheriff’s deputies responded to a suspicious person call at the residence at 10:30 p.m. Friday, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said in a statement. “When deputies arrived they made contact with the private security detail on the property,” the department said. “The individual who was outside of the property upon our arrival was warned and advised by deputies to leave the premises and left voluntarily without incident.” The department added that a trespassing report was taken, but no arrests were made. The Malibu Lost Hills deputies will increase patrols in the area as a precaution, the department said. The incident was first reported by TMZ. The incident at Harris’ home comes after President Donald Trump revoked her U.S. Secret Service protection last year. A senior White House official who confirmed the news last August noted that vice presidents typically only get six months of protection after leaving office. That timeline is accurate, as Congress passed a bill in 2008 that cleared Secret Service details for former vice presidents, their spouses and their children under age 16 for up to six months, beginning after the vice president left office, though then-President Joe Biden signed a memorandum in January 2025 extending Harris’ protection to 18 months.

articles.title: Sullivan, Peltola face off in fish-focused debate
articles.summary: Incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and opponent former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) faced off in their first head-to-head debate Saturday, which centered on the state’s fishing industry In a moment that the Peltola campaign has already capitalized on with social media posts, the two Senate candidates were asked in a speed round about the effectiveness of…
articles.body:
Incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and opponent former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) faced off in their first head-to-head debate Saturday, which centered on the state’s fishing industry

In a moment that the Peltola campaign has already capitalized on with social media posts , the two Senate candidates were asked in a speed round about the effectiveness of the North Pacific Fishery Management Council and NOAA Fisheries.

Peltola almost immediately raised her padel to the “no” side while Sullivan did not respond for a few moments. Before he responded, Sullivan appeared to glance at Peltola’s padel before flipping it to the “no” side himself.

“Happy to help, Dan,” Peltola wrote on social media after the debate.

The debate exclusively focused on the Last Frontier’s fishing industry, demonstrating its importance to the state’s economy.

Petola said she wanted to tackle the growing gas prices for fishermen if she were to be elected.

“This is the number one cost for all fishermen, this war in Iran is driving up our gas and diesel prices,” Peltola said during the debate.

Sullivan said he wanted to start “with the ban on the bad actors, banning Russian and Chinese trawl caught fish coming into the United States.”

In 2022, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration reported Alaska’s fishing industry suffered a $1.8 billion loss – a nearly 50 percent decline in profitability.

The industry has remained important in Alaska as the state was the country’s largest seafood exporting state, shipping more than $2.5 billion in domestic seafood exports abroad in 2025, according to the U.S. Trade Representative’s Office .

Alaska is a solidly red state, but has also shown an openness to independents and moderate Democrats. Peltola won three elections for the Last Frontier’s lone House seat and independent Bill Walker was elected governor in 2014, while Mark Begich was the last Democrat to win a Senate race in Alaska, doing so in 2008.

Peltola’s entry into the race was seen as giving Democrats a fighting chance in the state, with Cook Political Report shifting the race to a toss-up and citing Peltola’s campaign as a major reason behind the decision. Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) similarly rates the race as a toss-up as well and predicts Democrats are narrowly favored to win.

Peltola also outraised Sullivan in the second quarter of the year, with nearly $7 million to the incumbent’s $2 million, though Sullivan ended with more cash in the bank.

articles.title: Wisconsin GOP governor candidate swims from sinking plane after emergency lake landing
articles.summary: Wisconsin Republican Tom Tiffany says he and the pilot swam from a sinking Bonanza after an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau Saturday night.
articles.body: Wisconsin Republican gubernatorial candidate and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany said he and a pilot escaped with minor injuries after their small plane lost power and made an emergency landing in a lake Saturday night. Tiffany said the four-seat Bonanza was approaching Wausau Downtown Airport when it lost power following his appearance at the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner. "The pilot made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau," Tiffany wrote on X. COAST GUARD PLANE WITH DHS SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN ON BOARD MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER ENGINE FAILURE The congressman explained that he and the pilot quickly called 911 after hitting the water, but the aircraft began filling and sinking into the lake before rescuers could reach them. "As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat," Tiffany said. MULTIPLE INJURED AFTER FLOATPLANE MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING, CATCHES FIRE OFF WASHINGTON COAST Tiffany and the pilot were pulled from the lake and transported to Aspirus Wausau Hospital. Both sustained only minor injuries, according to the congressman. "I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly," Tiffany said. "They got us safely off the water and transported us to Aspirus Wausau Hospital, where we received excellent care." Tiffany shared that his wife, Chris, was by his side at the hospital following the harrowing landing and water rescue. "God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side," he said. "An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is." Prayers and messages of relief poured in across social media after Tiffany shared details of the close call. ‘COMMON SENSE AGAINST CRAZY’: TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SOUNDS ALARM ON SOCIALIST HONG IN WISCONSIN RACE "My god! What an ordeal. Very grateful everyone is safe," one person wrote. "Very glad you are okay, Congressman Tiffany," another commented. "Prayers to you and everyone aboard that flight!" a third person wrote. "So thankful you are all alive and able to see your loved ones." Tiffany currently represents Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District and is running as the Republican candidate for governor in the state's upcoming election. articles.title: GOP rising star reveals how Republicans can lock down minority voters without Trump on ballot
articles.summary: T.W. Shannon says Donald Trump transformed the GOP into a working party, pointing to job creation and lower crime as keys to winning Black voters.
articles.body: DALLAS — While President Donald Trump will not be on the ballot for the 2026 midterm elections, the former chair of Black Voices for Trump believes Republicans can maintain the momentum gained from his major performance improvements among Black voters during the 2024 presidential race. T.W. Shannon, a former Oklahoma state House Speaker who served last year in the second Trump administration and is now the Republican lieutenant governor nominee in his home state, says that policies "the GOP has expressed," as well as the Democratic Party's leftward lurch, will help Republicans as they continue to court Black voters. Trump won 16% of the Black vote in the 2024 presidential election, according to a Fox News Voter Analysis, nearly double his total four years earlier. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB "It's because Donald Trump has transformed the Republican Party back into the working party. You see Democrats competing for the Black vote now. Something that you used to not see at all. They didn't have to, they just took it for granted," Shannon said in a Fox News Digital interview Thursday on the sidelines of the first ever GOP midterm convention. Shannon pointed to job creation and lowering crime rates during the second Trump administration and said, "These are things that actually benefit...Black voters and Black communities." He then took aim at Democratic candidates backed by or aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Look at what....the DSA is offering, you know, we're talking about raising taxes, we're talking about doing away with the Senate... disbanding the police," he said. "These are not things that are well received in the Black community." Democrats disagree with Shannon's assessment. "Black Americans are going to reject Trump’s billionaires-first, cost-raising agenda at the ballot box this November and elect Democrats who are fighting to lower costs and deliver for working families," a Democratic National Committee (DNC) spokesperson told Fox News Digital. The spokesperson added that the "DNC is investing critical resources to reach, register, and mobilize Black voters across the country. While the Trump administration continues to attack civil and voting rights, we are fighting to protect the core of our democracy." Shannon, a Lawton native who became his state's youngest and first African American House speaker in 2013, and the first member of the Chickasaw Nation to hold the office, is favored to win in November in solidly Republican Oklahoma. articles.title: Republicans cast Muslim Democrats as chief enemies in ‘dangerous’ midterm pitch
articles.summary: Republicans are elevating anti-Muslim rhetoric as a key part of their midterm pitch, prompting sharp rebuke from Democrats and political observers. The attacks ramped up at Republicans’ first-ever midterm convention in Dallas this past week, where a host of top GOP figures called out New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul…
articles.body:
Republicans are elevating anti-Muslim rhetoric as a key part of their midterm pitch , prompting sharp rebuke from Democrats and political observers.

The attacks ramped up at Republicans’ first-ever midterm convention in Dallas this past week, where a host of top GOP figures called out New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, two of the country’s most prominent Muslim American Democrats.

The attacks are part of a broader effort by the GOP to turn prominent Muslim figures on the left into national symbols of the Democratic Party, tying them to issues including immigration, crime and what Republicans, like Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), describe as the spread of sharia law. As Cruz used his convention speech to amplify concerns about sharia law in America, calling out Mamdani, El-Sayed and other Democrats, a shout of “he should be shot” could be heard from the crowd.

El-Sayed, who’s up against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in a battleground Michigan Senate race, has responded that he hopes Republicans would “call it out for what it is: a call to violence that ought to be condemned across the board.” Mamdani, who was commemorating the 25th anniversary of 9/11 in New York on Friday, has not responded publicly.

It’s unclear whether Cruz could hear the audience member from the stage, and he didn’t acknowledge the shout. But the moment stood out as the second day of the convention marked the first anniversary of conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s assassination with condemnations of political violence.

“It is deeply alarming and unacceptable that Senator Ted Cruz carried on with his speech amid loud, explicit calls to assassinate prominent politicians, including two American Muslims,” the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization in the country, said in a statement.

“Failing to denounce such dangerous rhetoric normalizes political violence and endangers public servants and community members alike,” the group added.

The Hill has reached out to Cruz’s office for comment.

Rep. Delia Ramirez (Ill.), one of many Democrats who ripped Cruz’s remarks online, wrote on the social platform X that “it is disturbing that calls for and threats of political violence against opponents are tolerated.”

“Senator Cruz had the opportunity to end the calls for violence, instead he riled people up. He owes Mamdani, El-Sayed, Talarico, and the communities they are fighting to represent an apology,” she added , referencing Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, a Democratic state lawmaker.

Republicans, however, say the strategy is not about religion but rather highlighting what the Democratic Party has become.

“This is the face of the modern Democratic Party,” Republican strategist Brian Seitchik said. “It’s not anti-Muslim, it’s anti-socialist. It’s not the faith that’s in question, it’s their anti-capitalist world view. These socialists are trying to denigrate American values.”

“Democrats would be better served if El-Sayed loses because if he wins it will empower the crazy left and we will see more of these anti-American, anti-capitalists around the country in 2028 and beyond,” Seitchik added.

El-Sayed does not identify as a democratic socialist, and he is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Democratic strategists told The Hill that Republicans are misreading the politics and that their strategy will backfire, especially in swing states like Michigan.

“The new wrinkle for them is [President] Trump actually had high support in the Muslim communities and they’re lighting that on fire again, which will hurt them in places like Michigan,” Democratic strategist Eddie Vale said. “And no amount of bigotry will overcome Trump inflation and new record gas prices every day.”

Democratic strategist Anthony Coley argued that Republicans have nothing else to run on in the midterms.

“When you can’t run on results, you run on distraction, division, and resentment,” Coley said. “Trump did that as a challenger in 2024. But now he owns a record — prices he promised to lower on day one, [Jeffrey] Epstein files he vowed to release, and a long list of broken promises he now has to answer for.”

“Democrats should call out the anti-Muslim bigotry for what it is, keep voters focused on that record, and offer a specific vision for what comes next,” he added.

During the convention, Vice President Vance — who called El-Sayed “very, very evil” at a campaign rally earlier this month — urged voters not to “give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”

Vance took aim at El-Sayed in particular over remarks about his family. The vice president last month said he’d struggle to “go back in time” and tell his grandfather about El-Sayed, whom he accused of advocating for sharia law. El-Sayed has stressed that he opposes any religious law “because we live in an America where you should have the freedom of your religion.”

“So do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no…” El-Sayed wrote on X last month, referring to second lady Usha Vance, whose parents are immigrants from India.

At the convention, Vance said El-Sayed looks at his grandfather and “sees the color of his skin, sees his background, and decides that he could never have loved my wife.”

A fired up Cruz took it a step further, saying that sharia law “has no place in America” and that it is “fundamentally inconsistent with the Constitution and we need to stand together and stop it now.” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) also promised to “fully ban sharia law” in Texas during his Thursday remarks.

Cruz, meanwhile, appeared to double down Friday in social media posts warning of a “red-green alliance” of communists and Islamists. He also replied to excerpts of conservative commentator Tucker Carlson’s newsletter, in which he defended El-Sayed over controversial comments about 9/11, calling Carlson “ Jihadi Tucker .”

Republican strategist Doug Heye said Republicans have no choice but to ramp up these attacks.

“The scores of extreme rhetoric from El-Sayed, Piker, and other DSA candidates gives Republicans an opportunity to do something they otherwise couldn’t — go on offense,” he said, referencing progressive Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.

“Given how Republicans ’ backs are to the wall on so many issues because of Trump, they have to take it,” Heye said.

But Raqib Naik, the executive director of the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), said the rhetoric “legitimizes” prejudice and hate against Muslim communities.

An August CSOH analysis found that El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Senate primary produced a “concentrated wave” of anti-Muslim sentiments online after observing a similar pattern last year, when Mamdani became the Big Apple’s first Muslim mayor.

There are roughly 5.5 million Muslims in the U.S., according to Pew Research analysis , up from 2.4 million in 2007 — about 1.6 percent of the total population .

And though Mamdani and El-Sayed are the most prominent Muslims on the left, there have been some standout figures on the right, including Mehmet Oz, who spoke at the convention this past week. Now the Trump administration’s Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services administrator, Oz’s 2022 primary win in Pennsylvania made him the first Muslim nominee for a Senate seat.

Naik said Democrats “have to a degree failed to come out against this bigotry in the strongest possible ways” and urged the party to “push back” against the rhetoric amid broader concerns about a rising threat of political polarization and violence .

“The danger here is that this rhetoric could translate into violence,” he said.

articles.title: Vulnerable House Republicans embrace Trump as GOP bets on defying midterm history
articles.summary: President Donald Trump urged Republicans to "pretend that I'm on the ballot," as vulnerable GOP incumbents rallied at the first-ever midterm convention.
articles.body: DALLAS — President Donald Trump is getting a much warmer reception from his fellow Republicans during this election cycle than his predecessor did from Democrats this time two years ago. Conventional political wisdom dictates that the party in power will suffer losses in Congress during a midterm election year. Americans who oppose the president's party are typically more motivated to vote than people who support their agenda. But the GOP is banking on the opposite effect. The first-ever GOP midterm convention featured back-to-back keynote addresses from the commander-in-chief, as well as speeches from his Cabinet officials, allies and members of Congress. "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump told his audience on Wednesday. Republican incumbents and candidates running in battleground districts this November also took the stage, and all speakers projected confidence despite Trump's own low approval numbers. DEMOCRATS TARGETING 12 ADDITIONAL RED DISTRICTS IN MIDTERMS PUSH TO RETAKE HOUSE "We ran together in 2024 on a ticket with President Trump, [Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa.] and myself — voters elected all of us to deliver real change and results, and we've actually been able to do that with securing the border and delivering historic tax relief," Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, R-Pa., told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the convention. "Now what we're seeing is in a midterm, we are actually going to defy the historic trends. Why is that? Because the Democrats are so far left they are totally out of touch." Republicans believe their warnings of Democrats' socialist insurgency will help them keep their majorities in the House and Senate this year, along with touting Trump's signature tax cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. HOW ONE NYC SUBURB COULD DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE HOUSE Mackenzie is one of Democrats' top targets in the election cycle, along with Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., in the suburbs outside New York City. "He's the President of the United States, and whether it was Joe Biden or Donald Trump, I've always shown up," Lawler told Fox News Digital. "You have to be able to engage with the president, and, you know, frankly, this is where I think the Democrats have made a very big mistake. They could get a lot more in terms of what it is that they want if they would actually engage constructively." Lawler, Mackenzie and Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., are the three vulnerable incumbents who took the stage during the convention last week. TRUMP HITS KEY BATTLEGROUNDS TO SELL TAX CUTS, BOOST GOP AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Lawler, for his part, introduced two residents from his district whose daughter was killed by an illegal immigrant in Chicago — a poignant symbol of what Republicans say could happen more often if Democrats win. Trump has also campaigned in each of their districts in recent months as he crisscrosses the country in a bid to keep control of Congress for the latter half of his final term. But it was not just vulnerable incumbents who appeared in Dallas alongside Trump. The two-day affair also brought candidates from across the country, even those running in tight races. GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’ "When people say that folks are running away from President Trump, I'll tell you I'm certainly not doing that. And let me tell you why: because he has made promises to South Texas, and he has kept them, especially when we look at border security," candidate Eric Flores told Fox News Digital. JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH' "My opponent, who said, you know, that the sleepy Joe Biden administration and the no-show border czar, Kamala Harris, were on the right track. Let me tell you firsthand, I was on Operation Guardian support, was a federal prosecutor on the border. It was a humanitarian crisis. President Trump, on day one, secured our border." Flores is running in a South Texas district currently represented by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas. Time will tell if the strategy pays off, but Democrats are already seizing on it in hopes that associating with Trump will sink GOP candidates like it did in 2018. TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO' "Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan and Scott Perry made their priorities clear tonight: they care more about Donald Trump’s cost-raising agenda than what’s best for the people of Pennsylvania," Pennsylvania Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale said in a statement. "After jetting all the way to Texas to champion an agenda of higher gas prices, cost-raising tariffs, and healthcare cuts, Mackenzie, Bresnahan, Perry and the entire PA GOP have proven that they’ll put Trump ahead of our Commonwealth every single time — and Pennsylvanians are ready to send them packing this November." articles.title: State of Texas: Paxton and Talarico in their own words
articles.summary: At the Republican party’s first-ever midterm convention, President Donald Trump called upon attendees in Dallas to support Ken Paxton in the upcoming Texas senatorial race.
articles.body:
New episodes of State of Texas are on KXAN or the KXAN+ app every Sunday at 8:30 a.m. Don’t want to wait? Scroll down to continue watching this week’s segments now.

AUSTIN (Nexstar) – At the Republican party’s first-ever midterm convention, President Donald Trump called upon attendees in Dallas to support Ken Paxton in the upcoming Texas senatorial race.

“I’ll be coming back to Texas because we have to elect Ken Paxton. We have to,” Trump said Wednesday at the convention.

Before the President spoke, RNC convention attendees heard from Paxton himself in a speech where he discussed tax deductions and “standing up for Texans” on affordability.

In late July, Paxton unveiled his Protecting the Texas Promise plan , which includes economic relief for first-time homebuyers, tax deductions on healthy living, healthcare expense tax relief, and doubling the child tax credit. He elaborated on this plan at Wednesday’s convention.

“I want every Texan to be able to buy a home, raise their family, and live a healthy life. That’s why I unveiled the Protecting the Texas Promise plan to put thousands of dollars back in your pocket,” Paxton said.

“So what does that mean for your family? It means you can own a home with a landmark $50,000 down payment tax deduction. It means a $25,000 tax deduction for medical expenses because no family should go bankrupt just for getting sick. And it means a healthy living tax deduction for gym memberships, nutrition plans, and yes, even doctor-prescribed GLP-1’s,” Paxton explained.

Paxton also took stabs at his opponent, James Talarico, warning Republicans about what he called Talarico’s radical policies.

“He is a democratic socialist who never met a tax increase he didn’t love. As a matter of fact, he voted to tax your income in Texas. We all love that. He wants to tax your tips. He wants to tax your overtime. And he even wants to tax your Social Security. California already has two senators. It doesn’t need a third,” Paxton said.

Talarico touts affordability plans, willingness to work with Trump to help Texans

While Republicans rallied at the convention near downtown Dallas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico led events in the area to spotlight his campaign. On Wednesday, his campaign held a “Love Thy Neighbor” food drive that Talarico said collected over 20,000 pounds of groceries to donate to Texas families.

“I believe in servant leadership. That’s what my faith teaches me, putting others before self,” Talarico told Nexstar Washington Correspondent Vinay Simlot, as he stood in front of a pile of donated food.

Talarico challenged Paxton’s claims that he would push to raise taxes for Texans across the board.

“I only want to raise taxes on the wealthiest people in this country, on the top 1%. I want to cut taxes for middle class and working class Texans,” Talarico said.

Talarico also discussed plans to tackle affordability if elected to the Senate in November.

“Day one, we could repeal these corrupt tariffs so we can drive down grocery prices. We could repeal the federal gas tax and the federal diesel tax, which would drop the price of gas by 18 cents a gallon immediately. We could reverse these corrupt political deals that are driving up health care costs across our state,” Talarico said.

Talarico also said he plans to work alongside Republicans if elected, including President Trump, to create policies that benefit Texans.

“I look forward to working with President Trump to deliver for the people of Texas. He and I agree on certain issues when it comes to affordability, lowering housing costs. importing cheaper drugs from Canada so that we can cut prescription drug costs. Those are areas that we agree on and I will work with the President to deliver for the people of this state,” Talarico said.

Abbott’s campaign attack on Hinojosa signifies new stage of midterm races

State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, D-Austin, won the Democratic nomination for Texas Governor on March 3. It took 189 days for the campaign of three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott to mention his opponent by name.

“Radical Gina would rather trans your kids than protect them, educate them, or prepare them for a successful future,” Texans for Abbott Press Secretary Eduardo Leal said in a statement. “Hinojosa is a rubber stamp for the Socialist Democrats and their gender insanity,” the statement added.

Tuesday morning’s news release attacked Hinojosa’s voting record on transgender issues, including against a 2023 bill to bar doctors from performing certain gender transitioning medical procedures on minors.

With 41 days until the start of early voting, Abbott is polling worse than he has in previous elections. Some Democrats believe his change of focus shows panic.

“Some may see this as bad… but this is good,” U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, said on social media. “If he’s attacking that means he’s nervous. People attack or mention an opponent when there’s a problem.”

Republican political strategist and data analyst Ross Hunt, who runs Hunt Research , feels Abbott isn’t in danger of losing — and that Hinojosa’s team shouldn’t be quick to celebrate.

“(Mentioning her) is not a sign of weakness,” he said, “but something that should make the Hinojosa camp worried.”

Jim Henson, a politics professor at the University of Texas and the Director of the Texas Politics Project, says there’s also one other factor — the calendar.

“It’s after Labor Day,” he said, “the campaign is going.”

Supreme Court ruling could help Paxton close fundraising gap to Talarico

While the race for U.S. Senate in Texas is expected to be close, the race for campaign donations, so far, has been one-sided. Federal Election Commission filings from the end of June show the campaign of Democrat James Talarico raised about $66 million. Ken Paxton’s campaign raised about $9 million.

But Paxton could benefit from a recent Supreme Court ruling. In June, the Court’s conservative justices struck down a 50-year-old federal election law that limited how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates running for the presidency or seats in Congress. The justices ruled those limits violate the First Amendment.

That ruling likely gives Republicans like Paxton an edge. The GOP currently holds a sizable national fundraising advantage and tends to have more big money donors. Campaigns like Talarico’s tend to rely on higher numbers of smaller donations.

articles.title: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC
articles.summary: High construction costs and the Iran war are threatening the key manifesto pledge, the housing secretary says.
articles.body:
There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC.

"Headwinds" including the Iran war and rising construction costs are making it harder to meet the key Labour manifesto pledge, Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

"But I'm definitely not giving it up," she said, and stressed that the government was "making a difference" through investing billions in social and affordable homes.

Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.

Labour promised to hit the target through building both private and social housing by the end of the current parliament, meaning summer 2029 at the latest.

This implied an average of 300,000 new properties would be needed each year - a rate of construction not seen in decades.

Rayner told the BBC on Sunday: "It's a slim chance, but I'm definitely not giving it up."

She said it was important to keep the goal - which she said had always been a "stretch target" - in place, but that she was "being honest with the public" that it would be difficult to achieve.

"The prime minister wants us to make sure we're building council houses. He's made that absolutely, fundamentally clear," she said.

"We're seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period" - although he has not provided details on exactly what this will entail.

BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives.

Rayner's predecessor in the role, Steve Reed, last year admitted a sharp surge in construction would be needed to reach the goal - but said he expected it would just about be met once the impact of planning reforms took hold.

Analysts have said reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government should help increase construction in the long term, including changing the rules on green belt development to increase the area in which homes can be built.

But some argue that construction is being held back by factors including high house prices relative to average incomes, higher costs due to global conflict and labour shortages since Brexit.

BBC Verify has been tracking performance against the target using government data on Energy Performance Certificates (EPC). Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.

Data for the 12 months to June 2026 suggested about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England that year, far short of the 300,000 needed to meet the target.

"When you have these fringe activists online talking about repealing the 19th Amendment or alienating women, it really doesn’t help," Cooke said. You're constantly seeing this cultural push in terms of where women stand today in politics." Tiffany Losee, director of fundraising for The Conservative Caucus, told Fox News Digital that Democrats are to blame for pushing out this agenda and associating it with the broader Republican Party. "You have to understand this is all a game to the Democrat Party," Losee said. "They’re going to push out anything that looks fringe on the right." articles.title: Tiffany suffers minor injuries after plane makes emergency lake landing
articles.summary: Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.), who is running for governor of Wisconsin, said Sunday he sustained “minor injuries” after his plane made an emergency landing in a lake. Tiffany wrote on social platform X that his plane lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport earlier Saturday night. The GOP lawmaker, who was returning home after…
articles.body:
Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.), who is running for governor of Wisconsin, said Sunday he sustained “minor injuries” after his plane made an emergency landing in a lake.

Tiffany wrote on social platform X that his plane lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport earlier Saturday night.

The GOP lawmaker, who was returning home after attending the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner, added that the pilot of his plane made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau.

“After landing, we called 911. As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat,” Tiffany wrote.

The Republican gubernatorial nominee expressed his “deepest gratitude” to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department and “all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly” on Saturday.

“They got us safely off the water and transported us to Aspirus Wausau Hospital, where we received excellent care,” the Republican noted, adding he and the pilot suffered “only minor injuries.”

Tiffany said, “God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side. An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is.”

Tiffany, the representative for Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District since May 2020, is running against Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley (D) in the Badger State’s gubernatorial race.

Tiffany, with an early endorsement from President Trump, cruised to victory in the GOP primary last month. Crowley, meanwhile, earned a narrow win over democratic socialist Francesca Hong, a state assemblywoman.

Crowley said Sunday he was “grateful to God” that Tiffany and no one else was hurt in the emergency landing, adding it “could have been a tragedy if not for the heroism of the pilot.”

Crowley wrote on X , “I wish [the pilot] and the Congressman a quick recovery and that they can find solace with their loved ones.

Early voting in Wisconsin starts on Oct. 20 and runs through Nov. 1, the Sunday before Election Day.

Tiffany and Crowley are running to succeed two-term Gov. Tony Evers (D), who opted against seeking reelection.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk, one year later: What he meant to Black America
articles.summary: Kirk was outlining the opposite doctrine to the soft bigotry of low expectations.
articles.body:
On Sept. 10, 2025, a rifleman ended Charlie Kirk’s life under a tent at Utah Valley University . He meant with his single shot to end the argument. A year later, the question for Black America remains: whether a people will be addressed as children of God or as a client class, paid for the wreck of their homes.

Kirk’s overture to Black Americans is a summons that has outlived him. “You don’t have to stay poor,” he used to say. “You don’t have to accept being worse off than your parents.”

That sentence is an act of respect. Kirk was outlining the opposite doctrine to the soft bigotry of low expectations. He insisted that “all communities will do even better when we stop living under” that soft bigotry.

“ Three things that will almost assuredly keep you out of poverty ,” he wrote: Get a job, graduate high school, and do not have children before marriage. Researchers have called this same path the “ success sequence .” Among Black millennials who followed it, 96 percent are not poor.

In 1959, Black poverty stood near 55 percent, yet more than three quarters of Black children were born to married parents. By 2023, poverty had fallen to roughly 18 percent, yet 69 percent of Black births were to unmarried mothers and only about 45 percent of Black children lived with two parents. As legal racism receded, the family fractured . Kirk would ask: If the cause is Jim Crow, then why did fatherlessness explode after Jim Crow died?

“When Lyndon Baines Johnson came in through the Great Society program and started to subsidize single motherhood, it hurt all communities,” he said. “We should be instead subsidizing nuclear families.” The check became a rival to the husband. A young woman could, in Kirk’s phrase, “get married to the government.” Black children in single parent homes are three and a half times more likely to live in poverty than than Black children in intact, married homes. Family structure is a civilizational fact.

Kirk did not deny slavery or Jim Crow. What he denied was that a nation that elected a Black president twice with large majorities is still just a plantation, only with better manners. “ If you show me a ghetto ,” he said in 2018, “I’ll show you somewhere a Democrat is in control.”

Prosperity was a household. He named the three M’s: marriage, mating, and mortgage. “When you get married, have kids, and have to afford your mortgage, you have more skin in the game of America’s future .” President Trump made that household conceivable. In 2019, the Black unemployment rate fell to 5.3 percent . The difference is a father at the table and a church at the end of the block.

“There is a God,” his friends remember him saying, “and it is not us.” ABC News reported that he had gained tens of thousands of Black supporters. At Kirk’s memorial, President Trump said, “Charlie was actually a master builder of people.”

I had given speeches with Kirk for candidates. I think now of that last afternoon at the Arizona Biltmore , the ballroom loud for Rep. Andy Biggs (R) in his race for governor and for Warren Petersen (R) in his race for attorney general. He moved through that hall, and later under the Utah tent, with a composure that carries the same grace Martin Luther King Jr. showed on the eve of his death in Memphis, when he said he had been to the mountaintop.

It feels surreal to write that sentence.

The promise of the country was “super simple”: work hard, play by the rules, marry, have children, and do not break the law. A check cannot replace a father. “If you have something based on merit,” he said, “I don’t care if it’s all Black, all Asian, all white.”

What does Kirk’s memory mean on this first anniversary? It means that love does not flatter a people. The first civil right is the right to be expected to be good. A boy is a soul, whether in Phoenix or in Baltimore. Souls are not funded — they are formed.

The unfinished work of this anniversary is the recovery of the household, the pulpit that still dares to say that God is God and that a man who begets a child owes that child his name. Kirk did not invent that creed. He had the nerve to speak it in rooms that had been taught to call it hate.

If Black America takes him at his word in this twelfth month, it will not be because a white activist conferred permission. It will be because the data, the churches, and the memory of better order already knew he was right, and because a people tired of being pitied has decided, at last, to be free.

The Rev. Jarrett Barton Maupin Jr. is a Baptist minister, civil rights leader, public intellectual, and political commentator and consultant from Phoenix.

articles.title: Live updates: Lawmakers set to return from recess; Trump attends golf tournament in Ireland
articles.summary: House and Senate lawmakers will return to Washington this week with a packed agenda before much of their focus shifts to the fast-approaching midterm elections. The House, meanwhile, will reportedly consider…
articles.body:
House and Senate lawmakers will return to Washington this week with a packed agenda before much of their focus shifts to the fast-approaching midterm elections .

The Senate is expected to continue talks over the budget resolution and hold a procedural vote on the cryptocurrency regulation bill , among other priorities. The House, meanwhile, will reportedly consider a Senate-passed Russia sanctions bill prior to departing again until mid-November, after House Republican leaders recently cut two weeks from the chamber’s September schedule ahead of the midterms.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is scheduled to appear on CNN’s “State of the Union” and NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday, while House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is set for an ABC’s “This Week” appearance.

Attention will also be on Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) this week as he is expected to return after a monthslong absence for health reasons .

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim American Democrat, is also set for a Sunday morning news show interview, as Republicans controversially elevate anti-Muslim rhetoric as a key part of their midterm pitch. El-Sayed is scheduled to appear on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

President Trump is wrapping up his weekend trip to Ireland by attending the Irish Open at his golf club in Doonbeg on Sunday. He is set to return to D.C. later in the day.

articles.title: Speaker Johnson says Congress could work with Trump to deliver $5,000 checks to Americans but there are no guarantees
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson said that Congress would “work through” President Donald Trump’s promise to give $5,000 to American adults if Republicans keep the House and Senate after the midterm elections.
articles.body: House Speaker Mike Johnson told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Congress would “work through” President Donald Trump’s promise to give $5,000 to American adults if Republicans keep the House and Senate after the midterm elections, but he did not commit to ensuring the president’s proposal was executed. “I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that, like I have to do everything else,” Johnson said, when asked whether he would commit to carrying out Trump’s promise. Johnson said “it takes some time,” pointing to Republicans’ slim majorities. “I never go out and give big commitments on the front end because I’ve got to work through it, and that’s what we do every single day,” he said. “President Trump promised that to voters, though,” said moderator Kristen Welker. “You’re not willing to double down on that promise?” Johnson replied, “I’ll work with the president hand in hand, as I do all the time, and we’ll deliver for the American people.” “That’s the promise,” he added. At Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, Trump spoke on both nights, making a promise to the American people on Wednesday to issue $5,000 checks called the “Trump dividend” if Republicans do well in the midterms. The move sparked concerns from from Democrats, some Republicans and economic experts. Critics have characterized the president’s promise as an attempt to bribe voters and said that the move would drive up inflation. “So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000. It will be called the Trump dividend,” the president told attendees. Asked later whether Congress would need to approve such a disbursement of funds, Trump told CBS News, “We think not,” but added: “I think they will do it if we needed it.” Economic experts have warned that the proposal, if it comes to fruition, could add to the country’s towering debt and drive up inflation. Some Republicans, like Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, have issued similar warnings. Sending $5,000 payments to every U.S. adult could cost about $1.3 trillion. Asked why he would want to add to the national debt, Johnson said, “I don’t want to add to that.” He argued that “we’re not going to get further in debt if this idea was implemented.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said last week that the money would not be paid for with taxpayer dollars. Instead, Lutnick said that the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out.” It’s unclear how this would work. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., sidestepped a question Thursday on Fox News about whether congressional Republicans would support such a measure. “Well, that’s a good question. And we’ll cross our bridge when we come to it,” he said. Johnson also addressed the war with Iran, which shows no signs of resolving soon. Congress controls the nation’s funding, but Republicans have largely been willing to provide the administration with requested funds. Asked whether the White House has a blank check to continue the war, Johnson said “no.” “The war is not continuing,” he added. “What we’re trying to do now is resolve what has already been a big success.” The U.S. and Iran, though, have continued sporadic strikes, while shipping across the Strait of Hormuz remains far below the levels before the war began. Higher gas and oil prices show no signs of relenting. A recent NBC News poll found that 69% of U.S. adults disapprove of the president’s handling of the war. The national average gas price sits at $4.31 per gallon, which is a $1.33 increase since the war began. Johnson acknowledged that “we got to make sure that gas prices are down at planet Earth,” adding: “That’s what the president works on every single day.” Last week, Trump said at the Republican midterm convention that the war would “be over very shortly after the election.” Asked whether he was confident the war would be over by the 2028 presidential election, Johnson said, “Of course, we certainly plan for that to be true.” “And I would like it to be done, of course, today, certainly before the midterm election. But that’s just about a little more than 50 days away right now, and so we’re going to be realistic about this,” he said, adding that the war was “a complex situation.” “We believe it’ll be resolved soon,” he added later. “The president says right after the election, and I certainly pray and hope that that’s right.”

articles.title: Trump gives Smithsonian days to replace 'strange modernist sculpture' with Founding Father
articles.summary: President Donald Trump demands a 30-foot George Washington statue replace the "Infinity" sculpture outside the National Museum of American History in Washington.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is calling on the Smithsonian to replace a decades-old modernist sculpture outside the National Museum of American History with a towering, 30-foot statue of George Washington. In social media posts late Friday, Trump said the "Infinity" sculpture that has stood outside the museum since 1967 "says nothing about America," while Washington, he argued, "more than anyone else, says everything about America." Trump also called for the museum to open a five-year exhibition honoring Washington that would run through Feb. 22, 2032, the 300th anniversary of the first president’s birth. INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION Trump also wants the Smithsonian to install an 11-foot statue of Washington in the museum’s Flag Hall by Constitution Day on Sept. 17. The statue was featured at the recent Freedom 250 Grand Prix race. "Immediately design and display a five-year exhibition worthy of the Life, Sacrifice, and Contributions of George Washington," Trump wrote. "Then, as soon as it is ready, install a 30-foot Washington Colossus where ‘Infinity’ stands today," he added. "Infinity," created by New York artist José de Rivera, was commissioned by the federal government and installed outside the museum in 1967. It is unclear whether Trump can order the Smithsonian to make the changes. The institution is outside the executive branch and is overseen by a Board of Regents that includes Vice President JD Vance, Chief Justice John Roberts, lawmakers from both parties and citizen members. Fox News Digital reached out to the Smithsonian for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Trump has repeatedly criticized how the Smithsonian presents American history, particularly as the country celebrates its 250th anniversary. EXCAVATION SET TO BEGIN ON TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S 250-FOOT TRIUMPHAL ARCH AMID LEGAL BATTLE In his posts Friday, he accused the National Museum of American History of giving too little attention to Washington and other Founding Fathers. Trump singled out Washington’s crossing of the Delaware River on Christmas night in 1776 and the American victory at Trenton, saying the museum does not give those events the attention they deserve. "He is easily America’s Greatest Hero," Trump wrote of Washington. "Without him, our Country and our Freedoms wouldn’t exist." Trump also criticized the Smithsonian’s recently ended Center for Restorative History, an initiative created to spotlight stories that have been excluded from the national historical narrative. Trump said the museum should instead create a "Center for American Heroes." "Tell the stories of Americans who faced great challenges, overcame them, built great things, defended our Country, made America better, and helped our Nation more fully live up to our Founding Ideals," he wrote. SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PRAISES OUTGOING SMITHSONIAN LEADER WHO WAS UNDER PRESSURE FROM TRUMP ADMIN Those criticisms have also led to action by the White House. In March 2025, Trump signed an executive order aimed at eliminating what the White House called "divisive narratives" and "improper ideology" at the Smithsonian. The White House followed this year with a report criticizing the Smithsonian, including what it said was a lack of attention to Washington and other Founding Fathers. In July, Trump ordered his administration to place signs outside the National Museum of American History telling visitors that some exhibits are inaccurate. In a statement last year, the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents said it was committed to keeping the institution nonpartisan and its scholarship free from political or partisan influence. The board also acknowledged that the Smithsonian "can and must do more" and directed its leadership to ensure museum content is unbiased. articles.title: Óscar Puente se enzarza con una política de VOX por Lorca: "Dos meses después lo matasteis por rojo y por maric**"
articles.standfirst: El ministro de Transportes responde a la concejal de Cultura de Valladolid en redes sociales
articles.summary: El ministro de Transportes responde a la concejal de Cultura de Valladolid en redes sociales
articles.body: El ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, reaccionó con contundencia a un tuit publicado por Irene Carvajal, concejal de Cultura de Valladolid. La política de VOX comentó en sus redes sociales unas declaraciones de Federico García Lorca. "'La fiesta más culta que hay hoy en el mundo'. Palabras de Federico García Lorca en su última entrevista con Luis Bagaría, publicada en junio de 1936 en el diario El Sol", escribió, texto acompañado de un vídeo de una jornada taurina. La respuesta del dirigente del PSOE fue directa. "Dos meses después lo matasteis por rojo y por maricón", aseguró el titular de Transportes. Óscar Puente ha continuado su exposición con más críticas duras: "Si hay en el historial de desvergüenzas de la derecha de este país un hito insuperable, ese es reivindicar a Lorca y tratar de apropiarse de su legado, después de asesinarlo y enterrarlo como a un perro". La publicación del ministro Óscar Puente, siempre activo en las redes sociales, ha generado una enorme cantidad de interacciones y comentarios tanto a favor como en contra. Irene Carvajal, en el momento de escribir esta noticia, no ha respondido al titular de Transportes de forma directa, pero sí ha vuelto a publicar un nuevo mensaje en su cuenta personal de X, antes Twitter. "A todos los violentos que me habéis insultado y amenazado por defender la tauromaquia como hecho cultural, en mi derecho a la libertad de expresión: vuestra violencia os deslegitima para la defensa de nada. 'Ladran amigo Sancho, es señal que cabalgamos', Rubén Darío", ha compartido la dirigente de VOX. Irene Carvajal también ha realizado publicaciones con citas de Ernest Hemingway y de Joaquín Sabina para apuntalar su defensa de la tauromaquia. "Un torero no puede comprobar nunca la obra de arte que realiza" es la frase del autor estadounidense compartida por la política de VOX. La del cantante Joaquín Sabina, según ha citado Carvajal, es la siguiente: "El que no quiera ir a los toros, que no vaya. Y que se dejen de tocarnos los cojones, que hay cosas más importantes. Pero que no hablen de ecología ni de amor a los animales, porque no conozco a nadie que los ame más que los ganaderos y los toreros".

articles.title: There are no more sunsets after 7 p.m. for these cities starting this week
articles.summary: Permanent daylight saving time is still possible, but it wouldn’t prevent the end of sunsets after 7 p.m.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Days are getting shorter in September , and many of us are about to see a major, albeit sad, benchmark associated with that: our final 7 p.m. sunset of the year.

Within the last few weeks, we’ve seen the final post-8 p.m. sunsets of 2026. The sun will not set after 8 p.m. again until at least late March.

Meanwhile, seven of the more than 60 cities analyzed by Nexstar have already seen sunsets shift to the 6 o’clock hour, with roughly a dozen about to experience the same trend.

Honolulu hasn’t seen the sun set after 7 p.m. since mid-August, but that’s largely attributed to the state’s observance of year-round standard time. For those with clocks set to daylight saving time, the first to lose 7 p.m. sunsets were Panama City, Florida, and Las Vegas, according to data from NOAA.

Among those set to have their final post-7 p.m. sunsets this week are Los Angeles, Chicago, New York City, and New Orleans.

In most cases, the sun won’t set after 7 p.m. until daylight saving time begins in March – at least for now (more on this in a moment).

The interactive table below shows when more than 60 cities will see their final 7 p.m. sunsets, and when they’ll see their first in 2027.

It is possible that these cities will see 7 p.m. sunsets again before March, despite the calculations.

The Senate, on recess until Monday, still has a bill up for consideration that would make daylight saving time permanent. The bill, the Sunshine Protection Act, has already passed in the House and received President Trump’s support .

If the bill were to quickly pass through the Senate, it’s possible that our clocks would not fall back in November. Under that scenario, we would see 7 p.m. sunsets return much faster.

Take Austin, for example. After its final post-7 p.m. sunset in mid-October, the Texas city won’t see such a late sunset until daylight saving time begins in March. If our clocks locked on permanent daylight saving time, Austin’s first sunset after 7 p.m. would happen in late January, roughly two months earlier than currently planned.

Nearly 40 other cities analyzed by Nexstar would also see their first sunset after 7 p.m. prior to the currently scheduled resumption of daylight saving time.

For now, though, our clocks aren’t locking on daylight saving time.

It’s difficult to say whether the Senate will take up the Sunshine Protection Act or if it has enough votes to pass and make daylight saving time permanent. Unless they act quickly, our clocks will “fall back” to standard time on November 1, the earliest possible date daylight saving time can end.

articles.title: Data center hysteria is our latest group chat gone wild
articles.summary: The author argues against the growing public panic surrounding data centers, suggesting instead that they be managed through transparent regulation and market-based utility rates rather than bans or subsidies.
articles.body:
Remember 2018, when every city council, major airline, and coffee giant suddenly decided that plastic sip-lids were the frontline of planetary salvation?

It was the great Plastic Straw Panic. Celebrities made somber videos, corporate PR teams scrambled, and public policy shifted on a dime. The entire crusade was built on an eye-popping stat repeated with absolute, religious fervor: Americans use 500 million plastic straws every single day . With 330 million Americans, that is roughly 1.5 straws per person per day.

It sounded scientific and was repeated by reporters and even the National Park Service . With institutions and people we trust every day without verifying, you might be shocked to learn that this estimate wasn’t the outcome of a peer-reviewed publication. It wasn’t even something derived from a trade association representing the largess of American straw manufacturing. Instead, the statistic was actually an environmental science project of a well-meaning nine-year-old kid in Vermont named Milo Cress .

Milo’s project was totally defensible for a fourth-grader. But major media outlets, international corporations and politicians took that number, ran it through the viral echo chamber, and regurgitated it without a single second of basic scrutiny. Overnight, a kid’s napkin-math guess became unquestioned gospel . In this form, it spurred legislation that put the weight of jail time and $1,000 fines behind it — as with a California bill .

We didn’t need bot farms in China or foreign influence operations to fall for it. We did it all by ourselves, the way humans always do — in the glorious, chaotic excess of the crowd.

Which brings us to today’s issue sweeping the country: the great data center panic.

If you’ve read the news lately, you’d think the shiny grey boxes powering our modern world are literal sci-fi monoliths coming to drain our rivers dry, suck the power grid down to its copper wires, and leave us sitting in the dark. Once again, dizzying numbers are being tossed around, hyperventilated over, and transformed into instant moral panics.

Look, these aren’t bad-faith arguments, and the people raising them aren’t evil. Falling for runaway numbers is just a classic human mistake—one of those weird collective hallucinations we fall into together and laugh about later as cooler heads prevail.

Because when you strip away the doom-scrolling anxiety, the reality of energy and water is quietly miraculous. Every time you flip a light switch or pour a glass of tap water, you are benefiting from the quiet, cumulative genius of generations of engineers, hydrologists and grid operators far smarter than any of us. As writer Charles Mann quips , we live like royalty and don’t know it.

Our modern infrastructure wasn’t built by panicking; it was built by solving tricky engineering problems with cool-headed design.

Data centers are big. They use a lot of juice, and they need cooling. Water and power are challenges in particular — they require real engineering, localized planning, and honest numbers. This is the norm for any major industrial effort — steelmaking or computer chip fabrication . Both of which, it should be noted, far outstrip data center water use .

So, what’s the revolutionary, radical solution to integrating data centers into American life? It’s surprisingly boring, and delightfully American: treat them like every other industry, make them deal openly, and expect them to pay their own way.

Bans and moratoria neglect far more effective toolkits for handling data centers. First, existing nuisance law already protects a neighborhood’s peace and quiet. Whether your 2 a.m. tuba practice or a data center’s operations, noisemaking is prohibited. These heavy-handed responses will more likely backfire than protect Americans.

At a base level, public policy should neither punish nor privilege data centers. Just as economic development incentives for stadiums and reindustrialization have failed over and over , communities trying to entice data centers into their backyards with undisclosed, unbounded subsidies are likely to find themselves poorer. These policies are fumbles wrongly advertised as game-winning touchdowns. Instead of favoritism, policymakers are best served by treating everyone the same.

On the question of driving up electricity costs, we should make sure data centers pay market-based rates and can bring their own generation, not be shackled to outdated monopolies. Data centers are sophisticated, large energy users. We should let them explore options like off-grid data centers , behind-the-meter generation , and continue expanding ways for data centers to be good grid citizens . All of these inject flexibility into an overly rigid energy industry.

America has never moved forward by fleeing in terror every time a new technology demanded a bigger plug. We’re at our best when we challenge each other to see the facts clearly, insist on transparency, and let established legal principles handle the heavy lifting.

Put down the pitchforks and leave panic in the past. We can protect our communities, demand that big tech pays its bar tab, and build the future. And we can do it all at the same time by trusting in proven American institutions.

Josh T. Smith is the senior fellow for abundance and environment & natural resources at Pacific Legal Foundation. Megan Jenkins is PLF’s strategic research director.

articles.title: Election chaos in this red state just got even stranger for Republicans after Supreme Court ruling
articles.summary: The Supreme Court blocked Missouri's new congressional map, forcing the state to use 2022 boundaries that favor Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City district.
articles.body: Republicans suffered a fresh blow in Missouri after the Supreme Court blocked a congressional map that could have helped the GOP gain another House seat in November. The ruling, handed down last week, means Missouri will use its 2022 congressional map instead of the new boundaries backed by President Donald Trump and Missouri Republicans. Missouri held its August primary under the new map, meaning candidates won their party nominations based on one set of district boundaries. But those boundaries will change before the November election, when Missouri is expected to return to its 2022 map. TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE Typically, states redraw their congressional and state legislative districts once every decade after the Census to account for population changes and ensure that each district has roughly the same number of residents. The new map would have shifted parts of Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s Kansas City district into more Republican-leaning areas, making the seat more competitive. Republicans hoped the changes would help them win seven of Missouri’s eight House seats in the November midterm elections. The GOP currently holds six of the state’s eight seats, while Democrats hold two. Missouri must now use the 2022 map, which keeps Cleaver’s district more favorable to Democrats. The Supreme Court’s decision came after more than a year of legal battles over which congressional map Missouri should use. Missouri held its August primary under the new map, but the state will use its 2022 district boundaries for the November general election. That means some voters could be assigned to a different congressional district in November than the one in which they voted during the primary. The change could affect more than 1 million voters, or nearly one-fourth of Missouri’s electorate, according to an Associated Press estimate. The conflicting court orders have added to the confusion, with the November election just weeks away. Candidates and election officials must now adjust to the 2022 boundaries. articles.title: Trump’s coastal power grab should alarm all Americans
articles.summary: The right to manage the coast should remain equal under the law for all coastal states.
articles.body:
Environmental laws are often criticized for being one-size-fits-all mandates imposed on Americans who know how to govern their own affairs.

A prime example to the contrary is the Coastal Zone Management Act . Signed by former President Nixon, it empowers 35 states and territories along the coast and Great Lakes to advance their own priorities in federal decision making about the coast and ocean while standing up for local economies, natural resources and communities they know best.

Having administered environmental laws in state and federal leadership, I am extremely concerned how the Trump administration is manipulating this model law to impose a federal takeover of California’s coast. The best results come from state-federal partnership, not presidential fiat.

Arbitrary governance of the coast places our entire nation’s economy at risk. If coastal counties were a country, its gross domestic product would rank third in the world — behind only the United States and China.

A clean and healthy coast is an economic, cultural and ecological asset. Gambling with it to benefit currently favored industries is foolish, sacrifices the freedoms of nearly 130 million coastal Americans , and risks needless economic harm. The administration must chart a smarter course.

Under the guise of expanding offshore oil drilling and space launches , along with the establishment of seabed mining , this effort is supported by some of my Republican friends. But political pendulums inevitably swing, and this short-sighted initiative creates a dangerous power grab for future presidents of any political stripe to exploit.

It began when Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ordered the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to reopen the routine evaluation of California’s coastal management program done, but not finalized, under the Biden administration. Lutnick’s order, citing economic factors and favoring select industries, signals this duplicative review is rigged.

The Coastal Zone Management Act grants coastal states authority to balance national interests with their distinct priorities. Following certification by NOAA, states assess and shape proposed federal plans and projects affecting their coastal zones.

With this authority, California has successfully worked alongside 10 presidents to manage its coast as an economic engine and iconic natural feature attracting visitors and entrepreneurs from around the world. As it grew into the world’s fourth largest economy , California also expanded access to its coast, preserved coastal parkland and wildlife, and ensured local governments have a voice in the approval of federal projects, including subsea fiber optic cables, offshore oil and gas production, and military training exercises.

This is what Californians stand to lose. So, let’s consider Lutnick’s claims that the state blocks the nation’s economy and innovation.

Over nearly 50 years, California has reviewed more than 3,700 federal actions impacting its coast and, in 96 percent of cases , either negotiated improvements or approved projects as submitted. Clearly, the state-federal partnership has worked.

Furthermore, as the home of Silicon Valley, California creates tomorrow’s technologies. It is the foremost destination for venture capital, drawing three times more than the rest of the nation combined during the first half of this year. The state also ranks second for commercial space launches and seventh for crude oil production. These achievements have occurred while protecting nearly 22 percent of its coastline as state parkland and growing a $60.5 billion coastal economy supporting more than 600,000 jobs built on tourism, recreation, transport and fishing.

This formula for success falls apart if Washington can supplant California’s priorities with its own, especially if the Trump administration’s rush for new offshore drilling results in oil spills. We’ve seen time and again that such spills close fisheries, beaches and harbors, and transform vibrant coastal communities into ghost towns overnight.

In this context, the administration’s review of California reflects an approach less interested in facts and science than one focused on delivering a specific outcome for this president, who stands to gain significant power over 840 miles of coast just by changing California’s standing under the Coastal Zone Management Act.

There is more: The Trump administration is targeting California because the state’s coastal management is widely recognized as the nation’s best and strongest. If it falls first to a federal takeover, then like dominos, other states will easily follow, destroying one of our best examples of federalist governance.

This should alarm every American. Our love of the ocean is universal, so the right to manage the coast should remain equal under the law for all coastal states. Instead we see the administration play favorites, demonstrated by the abandonment of its oil drilling plans off the Atlantic coast after significant opposition from the region’s Republican leaders .

As the old saying goes, Washington doesn’t have a monopoly on wisdom. Hopefully, we won’t have to relearn this lesson the hard way.

Christine Todd Whitman served as governor of New Jersey from 1994 to 2001 and administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency from 2001 to 2003.
