articles.title: Irene Montero propone 1.800 euros de salario mínimo: ¿cuál es el SMI en otros países?
articles.standfirst: El SMI que propone estaría cerca de Francia, pero todavía lejos de Alemania o Reino Unido
articles.summary: El SMI que propone estaría cerca de Francia, pero todavía lejos de Alemania o Reino Unido
articles.body: Irene Montero ha lanzado una nueva propuesta laboral con la mirada puesta en las próximas elecciones generales. La que fuera ministra de Igualdad ha dado un paso al frente en Podemos y ha planteado una batería de medidas centradas, en gran parte, en el mercado de trabajo. Entre ellas destacan dos: elevar el salario mínimo hasta los 1.800 euros mensuales y reducir la jornada laboral hasta las 30 horas semanales. Dos cambios que supondrían una transformación importante respecto a las condiciones laborales actuales en España. La propuesta de elevar el salario mínimo hasta los 1.800 euros situaría a España en una posición diferente dentro del mapa europeo. Aunque seguiría lejos de algunos de los países con los salarios mínimos más elevados, se acercaría a los niveles de Francia. Los datos recogidos por Expansión muestran grandes diferencias entre países. Suiza aparece con uno de los salarios mínimos más elevados, con unos 4.548 euros. Le siguen otros países como Mauricio, Luxemburgo y Reino Unido, con cifras que se sitúan entre los 3.079 y los 2.512 euros. Por debajo aparecen países como Australia, Alemania, Países Bajos, Fiyi, Bélgica, Nueva Zelanda, Canadá y Francia. En este contexto, un salario mínimo de 1.800 euros permitiría a España recortar distancias con algunos de los países europeos que actualmente se encuentran por encima. Francia sería uno de los referentes más cercanos. España se encuentra actualmente por detrás de países como San Marino, Mónaco, Israel y Eslovenia, aunque las comparaciones deben hacerse teniendo en cuenta que no todos los países utilizan el mismo sistema de salario mínimo nacional. Con los 1.800 euros planteados por Irene Montero, España daría un salto significativo en esta clasificación. Sin embargo, todavía estaría lejos de los niveles de países como Alemania o Reino Unido, donde el salario mínimo se encuentra en una posición superior.

articles.title: Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop doing 'one thing' during attacks on Russia
articles.summary: President Donald Trump told reporters he wants Volodymyr Zelensky to stop hitting Russian diesel refineries, saying the strikes are causing a global fuel shortage.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has a blunt message for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Kyiv continues targeting Russia: Stop hitting its diesel refineries. Trump made the remarks Sunday while attending the Irish Open at his golf club in Doonbeg, Ireland, after a reporter asked whether he had spoken with Zelenskyy following a recent conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin. "Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told reporters. TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Trump said Ukraine could continue pursuing other targets inside Russia but urged Zelenskyy to steer clear of the country’s diesel infrastructure. "Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel because he's causing a shortage of diesel," Trump said. "This isn't done by the Middle East. This is done by what's happening with Russia and Ukraine." The president said he had already spoken directly with Zelenskyy about the issue. "So we spoke to Mr. Zelensky about it. There are plenty of other targets," Trump said. "Don't hit diesel fuel because that's hurting the world. We don't want him to hit diesel fuel. He's hitting diesel refineries." WATCH: FIGHTS BREAK OUT AT RUSSIAN GAS STATIONS AS PUTIN ADMITS FUEL SHORTAGES Trump’s remarks come as Ukraine has targeted Russia’s oil and gas infrastructure with long-range strikes, part of Kyiv’s effort to hamper an industry that provides revenue and fuel for Moscow’s war effort. Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago. The strikes have put pressure on Russia’s fuel supplies, prompting rationing in parts of the country and a Russian ban on diesel exports in July. The disruption has also added pressure to global diesel supplies, which have faced additional strain amid reduced oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Diesel prices in the U.S. climbed above an average of $6 per gallon on Friday, reaching a record high. Russia has intensified its aerial attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, including strikes involving ballistic missiles and drones, while Ukraine has continued targeting sites inside Russia. articles.title: In the rush to regulate police surveillance, slow down
articles.summary: In an op-ed, Greg Newburn warns against the trend of rapid legislative reactions to police surveillance technology, arguing that lawmakers should prioritize careful regulation over reactionary bans driven by political pressure.
articles.body:
President Reagan once said that the nine most terrifying words in the English language are: “I’m from the government, and I’m here to help.” He might have chosen: “We need to do something right now.” When a crisis occurs, or a high-profile story captures the public’s attention, voters demand action. Politicians tend to comply because the reward for acting quickly exceeds the payoff for getting the policy right. Today, we are watching this story repeat itself in the rapidly escalating debate over police surveillance technology.

By the count of one antisurveillance group, roughly 90 communities cut ties with Flock Safety , the nation’s largest vendor of license plate readers, last month alone, a fourfold jump from the month before. Citing fears of a “ surveillance state ,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) ordered the removal of all license plate readers from state highways, and Texas halted state funding for the cameras , putting Republican governors in the same “De-Flock” camp as a number of progressive city councils.

To be clear, hitting the pause button to evaluate a contract with a tech provider might be prudent. But preemptive bans, vows to oppose cameras under any circumstances, and calls to prohibit the use of federal funds to purchase this technology are panic moves that shut the door on careful policymaking before the work has even begun.

Public policy is littered with the wreckage of legislative panic attacks. In 1986, public outcry following the overdose death of college basketball star Len Bias led a bipartisan Congress to rush into law draconian mandatory minimum sentencing laws and the now infamous 100:1 crack-powder sentencing disparity. In 2001, the trauma of 9/11 gave us the Patriot Act, signed into law before most lawmakers even had time to read it. And within months after George Floyd’s murder in 2020, at least 20 major cities had cut police budgets by a combined $840 million.

Lawmakers were not wrong to respond to these real problems. The mistake was conflating the reasonable conclusion that “something should be done” with the pernicious demand that “something must be done right now.” Crises force lawmakers to make critical policy decisions when they are under the greatest pressure to act and have the least space to think. That’s exactly the trap the current surveillance debate has fallen into.

As before, the concerns are valid. New technologies that can deter crime and catch criminals can also create serious risks to privacy and due process. The Patriot Act is a case study of the dangers of unchecked surveillance power. But it also demonstrates the danger of making rash decisions about government authority under conditions of fear and misplaced urgency. The lesson of 2001 should not be to repeat the mistake in reverse, but to deliberate carefully about which uses are legitimate and what safeguards they require.

Even when lawmakers revisit rushed policy decisions, the damage is often already done. Congress waited nearly a quarter century before reducing the crack-powder sentencing disparity; thousands of people had served sentences policymakers later acknowledged made little sense. The retreat from “defund the police” came faster, thankfully. Within a year or two, many cities had restored their budgets as violent crime surged. Governments can reverse course, but they cannot return what was lost in the meantime.

There is one more reason to resist turning today’s fears into permanent law. Technology is constantly evolving. These tools will improve in accuracy and capability, and a framework that can evolve alongside them is worth far more than a categorical ban based on today’s relatively crude versions.

Law enforcement surveillance poses difficult questions. Good answers won’t come out of ideological food fights on social media. They will be found in the unglamorous work of developing reasonable regulations in light of costs and benefits. What legitimate public safety problem does a given technology address? What specific risks does it pose, and to whom? How do those risks compare with the benefits? And what, if any, safeguards can tilt the balance favorably? When politicians trade careful deliberation for instant gratification, they all but guarantee major missteps that will need correction later. In the debate over police surveillance, governing well requires the courage to slow down.

Greg Newburn is director of criminal justice at the Niskanen Center. His work focuses on improving the effectiveness and efficiency of criminal justice systems with the goal of reducing crime and punishment.

articles.title: Jeffries does not rule out pursuing Trump impeachment if Democrats win House
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Sunday he has not ruled out pursuing the impeachment of President Trump if Democrats take back the House in November. “No, we haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out in terms of impeachment,” Jeffries told George Stephanopoulos on ABC’s “This Week,” when the host asked…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Sunday he has not ruled out pursuing the impeachment of President Trump if Democrats take back the House in November.

“No, we haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out in terms of impeachment,” Jeffries told George Stephanopoulos on ABC’s “This Week,” when the host asked him whether House Democrats would pursue impeachment on day one if they are in the majority.

The New York Democrat noted Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the respective ranking members of the House Judiciary and Oversight panels, will lead the charge on holding the Trump administration accountable if they chair those committees come January.

“Both of them are doing a tremendous job,” Jeffries said. “We’ve got to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution, and then let the chips fall where they may, in the best interests of the American people.”

The House impeached Trump twice during his first term, first in 2019 over his threat to withhold military aid to Ukraine if the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, did not investigate then-presidential candidate Joe Biden.

The lower chamber then impeached Trump again after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. The Senate acquitted the president both times .

Trump said last month he expects Democrats to impeach him if they take back the House.

“They’re going to impeach me. They have no idea why,” the president said at a rally in South Carolina alongside Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.).

As of Friday, Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 68 percent chance of retaking control of the House. The minority party needs to flip a net of three seats to take back the gavel.

As for his caucus’s other priorities if they were to secure a majority in November, Jeffries highlighted three: nullifying Trump’s tariffs on foreign trading partners, forcing the president to wind down the six-plus-month Iran war and “restoring” Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the start of this year.

“These are some of the things that I think we can begin to do, but it’s going to have to be a bold, aggressive legislative effort that we sustain, not just for the first 100 days, but for the first year and the entirety of the Congress,” the House Democratic leader told Stephanopoulos.

articles.title: Lawler deflects on supporting Trump’s $5K dividend pledge: ‘How do you pay for it?’
articles.summary: Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) on Sunday joined multiple Republican lawmakers in questioning the fiscal sense of President Trump’s proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult. During an interview on ABC’s “This Week,” Lawler initially avoided the question of whether he supported Trump’s proposed dividend. “I support putting money back in the pockets of hard-working…
articles.body:
Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) on Sunday joined multiple Republican lawmakers in questioning the fiscal sense of President Trump’s proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult.

During an interview on ABC’s “ This Week ,” Lawler initially avoided the question of whether he supported Trump’s proposed dividend.

“I support putting money back in the pockets of hard-working Americans,” Lawler told host George Stephanopoulos, pointing to his support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which increased the state and local taxes deduction from $10,000 to $40,000.

Trump pledged Wednesday to send $5,000 to each of the roughly 270 million American adults if Republicans hold on to their slim majorities in both chambers of Congress in November.

The president noted recipients would only be able to spend the money in the U.S., but did not provide any other specifics.

“Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas.

On Sunday, Lawler noted Trump and former President Biden signed legislation providing Americans with stimulus checks amid the COVID-19 pandemic.

“The question is, how do you pay for it? How do you be able to pass the legislation to put more money back in the pockets of hard-working Americans? That’s the objective,” the moderate Republican told Stephanopoulos.

“Whether you call it a stimulus check or a dividend, the question is, how do you pay for it? That’s my focus. We have a $40 trillion debt and we have to be serious about tackling that,” Lawler later noted.

Multiple GOP lawmakers have pushed back on Trump’s proposal. Outgoing Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) was among them, arguing the dividends would lead to government “dependency,” which he called evil.

Vice President Vance said Wednesday on Fox News’s “ Hannity ” that the administration could tap into tariff revenue to fund such a program, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Thursday the administration will not utilize taxpayer money to dole out the dividends.

“Together we’re going to deliver that plan and we’re going to pay that money to the Americans, and not from taxpayer money,” Lutnick told NBC News , referencing the yet-to-be-launched Trump Platinum Card program for immigrants as a potential source of funding.

articles.title: Maine’s lobster industry finds itself squeezed on all sides amid Canada trade war
articles.summary: STONINGTON, MAINE — The Maine lobster business has found itself in the crosshairs of a trade war and congressional infighting as rising costs and other pressures leave the heritage industry in a precarious state. The war with Iran has sent diesel fuel prices soaring at a time when warming waters mean lobstermen are traveling further…
articles.body:
STONINGTON, MAINE — The Maine lobster business has found itself in the crosshairs of a trade war and congressional infighting as rising costs and other pressures leave the heritage industry in a precarious state.

The war with Iran has sent diesel fuel prices soaring at a time when warming waters mean lobstermen are traveling further offshore to look for lobster.

Profit margins have tightened significantly on the luxury good over the last 15 years, new research shows, while across the board, the industry is battling uncertainty.

“The cost now to just untie the boat is much, much more expensive than it has traditionally been. So it’s affected all of the gear, traps, rope, fuel, labor — I mean, everything that they touch — bait has gone up, everything’s gone up,” said Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association.

Nathaniel Lane, a lobsterman fishing off of Deer Isle, which includes the state’s most productive lobster port, said he’s joked with others in his profession that fishing trips have become a beautiful day for a boat ride.

“If you’re not profitable, all we’re doing is sports fishing,” he said at a recent talk sponsored by the Maine Center for Coastal Fisheries on the future facing the industry.

The price of lobster is at a 50-year low when adjusted for inflation, and while the crustacean is a splurge for the average consumer, many might be surprised by the slim margins under which Maine’s independent fishermen operate.

Alexa Dayton, executive director of the center, conducted a comprehensive survey on lobster economics to compare with one she first conducted in 2010.

The results show what she called a “gut punch” — a significant decline where in some cases boats are just barely exceeding their operating costs.

Boats of all sizes have seen profit plummet over the last 15 years, but it’s particularly true for boats of less than 25 feet, which now have just a 4 percent profit margin. Even larger boats in the 34- to 39-foot range have also seen their margins shrink drastically.

“The captain is fishing for free on many of these trips. Welcome to owning your own business, right?” she said.

“The boat gets fuel, crew is fed, bait’s been provided for, but the captain’s operating on a really low margin.”

It’s been a tumultuous few weeks for the industry.

Canada, already in a trade war with the U.S., threatened to respond to 50 percent tariffs imposed by President Trump with a 25 percent retaliatory tariff on U.S. lobster.

Such a move would be devastating for the Maine lobster industry, which is heavily intertwined with Canadian companies.

It also comes as Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) is fighting for her political life in a race that could decide the Senate majority. She’s criticized Trump’s tariffs on Canada.

Though Canada has a much shorter lobstering season, they have significantly more processing capacity, and Maine lobster is often peeled and packaged across the border before returning to the U.S.

Canada quickly backed away from the plan to impose tariffs on lobster, but it unnerved those who work so closely with partners across the border on a daily basis. It’s also unclear whether the matter could surface again given tensions between the two once-reliable trading partners.

“We’ve dodged another one, but it’s scary to be in the crosshairs of something like that that would really, really, really hurt individual businesses,” said McCarron.

The industry was also thrown into a congressional battle shortly thereafter, when retiring Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) crossed the aisle to back a procedural vote to take up several GOP bills, including one sponsored by him and a Republican lawmaker that would extend the period for adopting new regulations to protect the right whale, punting the matter from 2028 to 2035.

The whales have been killed in both ship strikes and entanglements in fishing gear. However, deaths have dipped significantly in the last two years , and the lobster industry notes that many of the entanglements have not been in lobster gear and occurred far beyond Maine, as the whales migrate up and down the Atlantic coast.

The legislation ultimately passed with 10 Democratic votes, but the party’s leadership was furious that Golden and another member gave up Democratic leverage in backing the GOP effort to bring forward the legislation with a package of other Republican-led bills.

“It’s a challenging topic in Maine, but obviously the lobster fishermen are a huge part of our constituency and have been worried a little bit about insufficient progress on this data before the deadline came down,” said Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), who represents the other of the state’s two congressional districts and backed Golden’s bill once it came to the floor.

“I think most of us are trying to make sure we have a way to save the right whale and the lobster fisherman.”

Maine’s lobster industry is hopeful that more time to collect data will show improvements in the current population of less than 400 right whales as well as shifting migration patterns that may lie largely outside of lobster territory.

It’s not clear if Golden’s bill will be taken up in the Senate, particularly with so little time in session between the midterms and the end of the year.

Dayton sees the proposal as a “doubled-edged sword.”

“We can track the whales now. We have a much better understanding of their patterns and where they are, and that’s informing the spatial question of where is the risk the highest,” she said.

The state and federal government have made significant investments in tracking the whales — funding that might lapse as a continued pause wouldn’t back the ongoing research the industry could use to make their case.

“They’re going to have access to all that great data that was collected through the monitoring program. If we don’t kind of jump on the bandwagon and go with the process and kick it out four or five years, we could be sitting here five years from now with no data, more whale deaths, and a much different regime and administration that will look at the rulemaking more stringently,” she said.

“It could be a worse outcome for the lobster industry four or five years from now than if we just take it on today.”

Maine has previously had some very good years for lobster, particularly between 2012 and 2018. But while some lobstermen may have made significant investments in infrastructure during that time period, the total number of lobster landings has been on the decline since.

“We peaked at a level that nobody ever thought was possible, and I think the resource was kind of settled back down into a new place. And that is not a place where if your price is just not helping you make ends meet, you can’t go out and fish harder,” McCarron said.

“There are only so many lobsters to catch.”

Lane said the future of lobstering will be one in which successful lobstermen will have carefully managed their finances and investments so as not to overextend themselves.

“I think there’s going to be an industry, but it has to be balanced between finding that sweet spot operationally. Who can continue to fish is going to be who’s kind of figured out the sweet spot between having the right equipment and having that equipment work for you,” he told The Hill.

“You’re going to have to be nimble enough to have a quality operation, but to make sure it doesn’t own you. You have to own your business, not let the business own you.”

Dayton fears, however, that current conditions could deter a new generation of lobstermen, while other shifts in the industry favor the biggest boats with more staff — undercutting generations of small family businesses that earn their living out on the water.

“This industry has been resilient and has adapted to change over 100 years, and I think that’s going to happen again,” but, she added, “uncertainty is not our friend.”

“Making room for the next generation is the biggest thing, in my view. That’s what we have to figure out is if you’re a young person today looking at all the news and saying, ‘Should I go be a carpenter or should I go be a lobsterman like my family did?’ … That’s my fear is that people will get sucked up in the uncertainty, and that next generation will choose not to commit to the fishery, and if we lose fishing here, we lose our place.”

articles.title: This Week on The Hill: Congress returns to a packed agenda
articles.summary: The Senate returns this week to a packed agenda, with lawmakers facing a trio of unfinished priorities: crypto legislation, the farm bill and the budget resolution that Republicans need to unlock a third reconciliation package. The biggest question hanging over the chamber is whether Republicans can get on the same page on the budget resolution.…
articles.body:
The Senate returns this week to a packed agenda, with lawmakers facing a trio of unfinished priorities: crypto legislation, the farm bill and the budget resolution that Republicans need to unlock a third reconciliation package.

The biggest question hanging over the chamber is whether Republicans can get on the same page on the budget resolution. Conservative fiscal hawks have railed against the lack of spending offsets in the package.

The chamber is also expected to take up a new version of a landmark crypto bill dubbed the Clarity Act, with a procedural vote slated for Tuesday. The legislation aims to establish a regulatory framework for cryptocurrency.

But it is not expected to win support from most Senate Democrats, who have long pushed for a provision restricting elected officials’ ability to profit from the industry.

The Senate Agriculture Committee, meanwhile, is expected to hold another vote on the farm bill, which would reauthorize agricultural and food programs for the next five years, according to Politico. The committee failed to advance the bill in early August, when Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) was absent.

The House is also set to return this week and take up a number of bills.

The crowded agenda comes as lawmakers face a shrinking legislative calendar ahead of the November midterms, raising the stakes for Republicans hoping to move their priorities while they still control both chambers of Congress. The coming week will offer an early test of how much the Senate can accomplish.

Senate to continue talks on budget resolution: Advancing the budget resolution will be key to unlocking a third reconciliation bill.

Senate Agriculture Committee to vote on farm bill: The legislation failed to advance out of the committee last month due to Republican absences and Democratic opposition.

Senate to hold procedural vote on Clarity Act: The legislation is not expected to garner Democratic support over the lack of an ethics provision.

House to consider Russia sanctions bill: The House will consider Senate-passed legislation that will impose harsher sanctions on Russia.

House to put Ratepayer Protection Act on floor: The lower chamber will take up a bill aimed at mitigating the impact of data center costs on household electric bills. It is expected to garner bipartisan support.

Senate tries to unlock reconciliation process

The upper chamber is trying to reach a deal on a budget resolution that would unlock a third reconciliation bill to potentially fund defense and intelligence, agriculture aid, and incentives for states to adopt Trump-backed voting restrictions.

The House passed its own budget resolution before the August recess, but Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) released his own version of the resolution and has been working on it over the recess.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) had repeatedly warned before the August recess that he doesn’t have 50 votes to pass the budget resolution, which is the first step in the reconciliation process.

And vulnerable incumbents like Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) have made clear that they don’t want to face another vote-a-rama, with the opportunity for Democrats to force them to take tough votes, before the midterms.

GOP leaders and conservative Republicans have been eyeing a third reconciliation bill as a vehicle to advance the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a long-standing conservative priority that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections and photo identification to cast a ballot.

Trump has been pressuring Thune to pass the budget resolution, arguing in a Truth Social post last month that the measure is the “first step towards getting as much of THE SAVE AMERICA ACT as possible in a Budget Bill, funding our Troops, and helping our Farmers.”

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, has previously said she wants more transparency about the Pentagon’s needs before the Senate votes on the budget resolution.

“We’ve heard so many different numbers coming from the Pentagon over the course of the last six months, so I really want to know what do they need,” she said last month. “I haven’t had anybody personally sit down and visit with me on those numbers, so I’m pretty skeptical that’s all they need.”

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee and the Armed Services Committee, said earlier this month that Republicans will likely move an omnibus spending package with emergency funding for the Pentagon and other priorities, and then move the separate budget reconciliation package with funding for the six-month conflict with Iran.

Senate Agriculture Committee takes another shot at farm bill

Sen. John Boozman (R-Ark.), the chair of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition and Forestry, plans to hold another committee vote on the farm bill this week, Politico reported.

“I really feel like it’s important to continue to have members express where they’re at on this, and so we are going to vote again next week,” Boozman told the outlet.

The committee failed to advance the legislation in August, amid Republican absences and unified Democratic opposition to the bill’s food aid provisions.

McConnell has been absent from Congress after he suffered a serious fall in June. His office said he will continue his physical therapy routine from home during the Senate recess period.

“It seems like Sen. McConnell is continuing to recover and doing well. So hopefully, we’ll get him back. We don’t have any assurance of that, but we do have the assurance that he is doing better,” Boozman told Politico.

Democrats on the panel, meanwhile, have pushed back against a provision in the bill that would require states to help cover the cost of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) funding, demanding that the implementation date be delayed by two years to allow states to reduce SNAP error rates. Boozman had offered a one-year delay, but the panel’s Democrats said this was not enough time.

Senate to hold procedural vote on Clarity Act

The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote Tuesday on an updated version of the Clarity Act, a bill aimed at creating a regulatory framework for cryptocurrency.

Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.), who chairs the Senate Banking subcommittee on digital assets, argued last week that Democrats have secured more than 100 revisions to the cryptocurrency regulation bill.

Her office pointed to 114 “substantive, distinct wins requested by Democrats and agreed to by Republicans” in a document shared first with The Hill. This included changes to the framework through which the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regulates digital assets, the application of anti-money laundering laws and the oversight of non-decentralized finance platforms.

“I’ve bent over backwards to make this a truly bipartisan bill that both sides can be proud of and which protects both consumers and this industry,” Lummis said in a statement to The Hill.

But still, Senate Democrats have pushed for a provision restricting the ability of elected officials to profit off the industry amid concerns about Trump and his family’s various crypto-related business ventures. And the updated version of the bill doesn’t appear to include that language.

“If this bill fails it won’t be because of ethics, it will be because Democrats didn’t join Republicans in embracing a bipartisan bill that protected consumers, cements America’s leadership in digital assets, and empowered law enforcement to clamp down on illicit finance,” Lummis wrote on X.

The House Rules Committee will meet Monday to consider a Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and backed by Trump.

If enacted, the measure would impose harsher sanctions on Russia and buyers of Russian oil and gas than the U.S. has previously enforced and extend existing sanctions on Iran, aiming to economically squeeze the two countries.

House GOP leaders are seeking to move the measure through regular order, meaning Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will need near-unanimous Republican support on a procedural vote to advance the bill on the floor. But it remains unclear whether Johnson has enough GOP votes to clear that hurdle.

And some Democrats have bristled at giving Trump tariff authorities even if they want to find a way to provide additional U.S. support to Ukraine. They argue that the president already has ample authority to impose sanctions on companies, individuals and oil tankers financing Russia’s war machine.

Reps. Don Beyer (D-Va.), a senior House Democrat of Congress’ Joint Economic Committee; Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; and Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the ranking member of the House Ways and Means Committee, argued in a joint statement last week that the bill would do “more harm than good.”

“This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable. These flaws would raise Americans’ prices while undermining support for Ukraine in the long term. We continue to seek bicameral, bipartisan negotiations to craft a bill that can win strong support in both chambers and deliver on our promise to Ukraine,” they wrote.

House to vote on Ratepayer Protection Act

The House will vote on legislation Tuesday, dubbed the Ratepayer Protection Act, that seeks to mitigate data centers’ impacts on Americans’ electric bills, according to Johnson’s office.

The measure, which aims to codify a White House pledge signed by tech giants earlier this year, forces state regulators to hold a hearing on a standard that would ensure that large data centers pay for the cost of new power or power lines stemming from their electricity use. It does not force them to actually adopt such standards.

“[I]t has become clear that across the entire industry there is one entity uniquely positioned to stand up for families and communities who are the ones paying electricity bills-and that is this Committee, and our colleagues in Congress,” House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) said in a statement.

The bill is slated for a vote under a fast-track process known as suspension of the rules, which requires two-thirds support in the House for passage.

But some Democrats on the House Energy and Commerce Committee have previously described it as a “first step” rather than a panacea.

Rep. Nannette Barragán (D-Calif.) said that the bill “recognizes an important principle,” but also said “this is not going to be enough. We need to do more to ensure that families are protected from higher electricity costs while also addressing the health and the environmental impacts.”
